metrics.name: fragment_vs_word_onset_similarity

regions.explanation: At 19.81s, the onset of “parties,” is repeated 3 time(s) before the word is completed (fragment-to-onset spectral similarity 1.00). Repeated onsets before the word is completed fragment it and interrupt the speech rhythm. Fix: Begin the word once, deliberately; a short breath before it helps.

regions.text: colors, from every section of this country, to
regions.explanation: From 27.82s to 31.62s (“colors, from every section of this country, to”), 2 pause(s) at punctuation shrank from 1.49 s to 90 ms on average. Pauses at punctuation mark the end of an idea and give the audience time to absorb it; running through them merges separate thoughts into one stream. Fix: Hold a clear pause at each punctuation mark, about as long as the reference.

regions.text: for freedom. So it was at
regions.explanation: From 51.75s to 54.65s (“for freedom. So it was at”), pitch range (10th–90th percentile) narrowed to 0.2 st from 4.5 st (-95%); that is 10.1× the reference speaker's natural word-to-word variation. Pitch movement is the main cue English listeners use to find the focus word of a phrase; with a flattened contour every word carries equal weight and the line sounds recited. Fix: Lift pitch on the focus word of each clause and let it fall at the end of the thought.

regions.text: Concord. So it was a century ago at Appomattox. So it
regions.explanation: From 55.76s to 67.81s (“Concord. So it was a century ago at Appomattox. So it”), articulation rate slowed to 2.32 syll/s against 3.97 syll/s in the reference (-42%); that is 2.1× the reference speaker's natural word-to-word variation. Stretched words without matching emphasis read as hesitation and dilute the rhythm of the phrase; the audience's attention drifts between content words. Fix: Tighten these words to the reference pace; keep length only on the stressed word.
